title: 27 Things That Make Your Classroom Management Plan Work gement-plan-work/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin lays out a reference list of 27 specific hallmarks that, taken together, make the SCM classroom management plan actually work -- ranging from an extreme focus on student independence and elimination of external rewards, to thorough teaching of rules, calm referee-like enforcement, and a spartan, pin-neat classroom. His framing argument is that the plan itself is only a small part of effective classroom management; the real leverage comes from the surrounding culture and teacher behaviors that make the plan matter to students by shifting their motivation from extrinsic to intrinsic. He closes with a pointed jab at critics who dismiss SCM methods based on a surface-level phrase without understanding the underlying rationale, quoting Alexander Pope's 'a little learning is a dangerous thing' to characterize shallow criticism of the approach.
points: A classroom management plan by itself is described as only a small part of effective classroom management; the surrounding culture is what makes the plan matter to students.
The real leverage in SCM comes from flipping students from extrinsic to intrinsic motivation, not from the plan's rules and consequences alone.
Hallmarks include a spartan, pin-neat classroom, economical teacher talk, and worthy praise only -- specific, concrete disciplines rather than vague philosophy.
Critics who dismiss SCM strategies based on a surface-level phrase without understanding the underlying rationale are compared to Alexander Pope's 'a little learning is a dangerous thing.'
quotes: Your classroom management plan is a small part of effective classroom management.
The magic is in making your plan matter to students. The magic is in flipping your classroom from one that is extrinsically focused to one that fires your students’ intrinsic motivational engines.
However, as a reference, listed below are 27 things—or SCM hallmarks—that when implemented a certain way cause students that want to listen, learn, and behave.
Some readers occasionally criticize one or more of our methods without knowing what they mean or how we define them.
In his 1709 poem An Essay on Criticism, Alexander Pope wrote that “A little learning is a dangerous thing.” This aptly describes much of public education.
